children: Heeding airlines’ call for an extension of relief measures on jet fuel, the Maharashtra government has extended the concessional 7 per cent value-added tax (VAT) rate on aviation turbine fuel (ATF) until April 14, 2027, even as sources tell businessline that a similar move is expected from the Delhi government soon.
According to a November 12 notification issued by Maharashtra’s Finance Department, the concessional rate on duty-paid ATF will remain applicable until April 14, 2027, instead of November 14, 2026.
The decision provides a five-month extension to the relief initially introduced for the period between May 15 and November 14 this year.
Accordingly, industry sources told businessline that the move will help stabilise airlines’ finances and provide them with headroom to contain airfares.
The development comes as ATF prices in Delhi stand at around  ₹138 per litre following the November 1 revision. This marked the fourth consecutive monthly increase in jet fuel prices.
Earlier, Maharashtra had reduced VAT on ATF from 18 per cent to 7 per cent, while Delhi lowered the levy from 25 per cent to 7 per cent. Both concessions were initially introduced for six months.
As reported by businessline earlier, the Federation of Indian Airlines (FIA), representing IndiGo, Air India and SpiceJet, had sought continuation of the lower tax rates in Delhi and Maharashtra.
Besides, in an October letter to Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta, the federation requested that the concession be extended beyond November 16.
FIA said the lower levy had encouraged airlines to purchase more fuel in Delhi, with ATF uplift increasing  40 per cent since the reduction.
It maintained that continued relief would support fuel sales and corresponding VAT collections.

Furthermore, the federation pointed out that fuel expenditure had increased to around 50–55 per cent of airlines’ operating costs, compared with the usual 30–40 per cent, affecting profitability and cash flows.
The industry’s request came amid the continuing West Asia crisis, with airspace restrictions forcing airlines to take longer routes and incur additional fuel and crew expenditure.
Additionally, longer flying hours have reduced aircraft utilisation, while rupee depreciation has increased the cost of foreign currency payments towards aircraft leases, maintenance and insurance.
Consequently, ATF price hikes and accompanying fuel surcharges led to higher airfares during the peak travel period, raising concerns over affordability.

A businessline report in October showed that one-way fares from Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru to Patna were quoted at  ₹25,000–35,000 for travel between November 4 and 15, against the usual  ₹4,500–6,000.
In addition, fares to Goa for December 20–24 were quoted at  ₹12,000–22,000, compared with the usual  ₹4,000–6,500.

title: Maharashtra extends 7% ATF VAT until April 14; Delhi likely to follow
